question.worked_solution:
To solve the equation $\sqrt{14-x}=x-2$ we raise both sides to the power of $2.$  This allows us to get rid of the radical, and gives us a quadratic equation that is easier to solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{14-x} & =x-2 \\ (\sqrt{14-x})^{2} & =(x-2)^{2} \\ 14-x & ={x}^{2}-4x+4 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+x-14 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-3x-10 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-5x+2x-10 & =0 \\ x(x-5)+2(x-5) & =0 \\ (x-5)(x+2) & =0 \\ x & =5,-2\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that in square root equations, we should always check the obtained value(s) to ensure that they are actually solutions of the original equation.

- First, we check whether the obtained value $x=5$ is a solution of the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{14-5} & \overset{?}{=}5-2 \\ \sqrt{9} & \overset{?}{=}5-2 \\ 3 & \overset{?}{=}5-2 \\ 3 & =3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Indeed, the value $x=5$ does satisfy the original equation.

- Second, we check whether the obtained value $x=-2$ is a solution of the original equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{14-(-2)} & \overset{?}{=}-2-2 \\ \sqrt{16} & \overset{?}{=}-2-2 \\ 4 & \ne -4\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

The value $x=-2$ does *not* satisfy the original equation, so we discard it.

Therefore, the only solution of $\sqrt{14-x}=x-2$  is $x=5.$
